The question this page answers

For firms, how serious a constraint is finance — and how does it compare with other constraints?

Firms: how much finance matters depends on the question and the firms asked

In a 2022 survey of formal firms in seven governorates, 22% named access to finance as a business challenge, against 50% for electricity and 46% for fuel shortages. Among firms in the report’s finance-obstacle tabulation, which excludes firms that said they did not need a loan, 91.84% rated financing obstacles as major or moderate. These answers, the credit paths of the few firms with a line of credit and what a programme reports for the firms it supported address different questions and cannot be merged into one national percentage.

Explore questionsOpen evidence
What this does not establish

What these figures do not establish

The 22% general-business challenge measure and the 91.84% finance-severity measure use different questions and bases, so they are not two estimates of the same national rate. The 18 valid loan-source responses describe only that small conditional group. Results reported by the Small and Micro Enterprise Promotion Service (SMEPS) describe the firms the programme supported; they are not national MSME prevalence and do not establish that the programme caused the results.

02Analysis

Finance in the context of other business constraints

Among formal firms in the seven-governorate 2022 survey, the shares naming each item as a business challenge were: electricity 50%, fuel shortages 46%, transport or road blockades 32%, tax administration or tax rates 30%, political instability 27%, access to finance 22%, siege 18% and practices of informal competitors 17%. Respondents could name more than one challenge, so the shares add up to more than 100%, and neither the exact question wording nor the base for this question is recorded in the evidence base; small differences between adjacent items should not be read as a fixed ranking. These results answer “what was cited as a general challenge in this survey?” — not “what is the national ranking of constraints for all Yemeni firms?”

Another view of the evidence
03Analysis

A different question produces a much larger finance number

Among the firms in the report's finance-obstacle tabulation, which excludes firms that said they did not need a loan, 68.71% rated financing obstacles as major and 23.13% as moderate — 91.84% combined. This is a result for that filtered group, not the share of all Yemeni firms facing a major or moderate finance obstacle.

04Analysis

Lines of credit are rare in this sample, and their source is known for only 18 firms

Within the formal-firm sample, 31 of 328 firms reported a line of credit from financial or non-financial institutions, and only 18 gave a valid response to the loan-source question. The source mix can therefore be described only for those 18 responses — not for all surveyed firms, all borrowers or all Yemeni enterprises.

05Evidence

Formal firms in this sample: most held a bank account, but banks financed almost none of their working capital

Among formal firms in the 2022 seven-governorate survey, 58.2% (191 of 328) reported a checking or savings account. Their working capital came mainly from internal sources: on average, 69.12% came from internal funds or retained earnings, 16.66% from money lenders, friends or relatives, 10.15% from advance payments by clients, 1.97% from non-bank financial institutions, 1.31% from supplier credit and 0.56% from banks. In a separate question on the financial intermediaries they use, 73.48% of responding formal firms named an exchange store or money exchanger and 24.39% a commercial bank; firms could name more than one, so these are not market shares. The evidence base does not hold the number of firms behind the working-capital averages or the intermediary question. Among the 217 informal firms surveyed, 80.18% had no bank account; that sample was drawn from activity and location lists rather than a national register. The formal-firm sample includes micro firms with fewer than five employees, and neither sample represents all Yemeni firms.

06What it means

What this means

The finance problem does not begin and end with whether a loan exists. The full journey includes the need for finance, application, approval or rejection, amount, terms, source, use, repayment pressure and what happened to the firm afterwards. Current evidence does not cover that entire journey nationally.

Another view of the evidence

More evidence and context

More detail on this question, each item with its own period and limits.
Evidence

Programme reach is useful evidence about the programme itself

The Small and Micro Enterprise Promotion Service (SMEPS) reports that in 2024 it supported 8,217 MSMEs and disbursed USD 22,865,322, and that across 2021–2024 its support reached 31,560 MSMEs with a programme total of USD 54.7 million; the evidence base does not specify whether this total is funding committed or funding disbursed. The 2021–2024 total is not established as a count of unique firms. These are programme-delivery measures for the firms the programme supported; they are not a count of Yemen’s MSME population, a measure of financial-sector lending, or proof of causal impact.

Evidence

A programme result is not a national rate

SMEPS’s 2024 Annual Report states that 19% of supported MSMEs accessed financial services in 2024, and gives 15% for 2021–2024 against a programme target of 40%. The report does not fully specify the calculation base or the operational definition of “accessed financial services”. The KPI can therefore be read only for the firms the programme supported, with that limitation visible: it is not a national MSME access rate, and the 40% remains a target, not an observed result.

Evidence periodWorld Bank Yemen Enterprise Survey, September 2022, seven governorates · SMEPS programme report for 2024
How can 22% and 91.84% both be right?
A 2022 survey of formal firms in seven selected governorates can tell us that finance was named less often than electricity or fuel, and also that most firms in a narrower group rated finance a major or moderate obstacle. The numbers do not contradict each other. They answer different questions.

What measurement would change the decision?

Measurement priorityP0 · Firms / MSME
A current MSME finance demand/use baseline
The 2022 Yemen Enterprise Survey (formal firms in seven governorates) and programme evidence from the Small and Micro Enterprise Promotion Service (SMEPS) can each be used within its own scope; neither supplies a current representative national MSME finance baseline.
Evidence needed: A representative survey of firms/MSMEs, or validated administrative data linked to firm-level data, with explicit definitions, covering finance need, application, approval or rejection, amount, terms, source, use, repayment pressure and outcome.
Decision it would strengthen: This evidence would show the finance journey from need and application through approval or rejection, terms, use and repayment pressure, while SMEPS remains a separate programme-evidence layer.
Open this measurement priority
Measurement priorityP1 · Credit infrastructure / MSME
Credit-infrastructure reach and actual use
Legal texts, project documents and institutional records can establish that credit infrastructure exists or is being developed; lender participation, inquiry use and borrower reach are not yet documented as one complete evidence chain.
Evidence needed: Administrative data from credit-information and collateral infrastructure and participating institutions on coverage, inquiries, report use, collateral registration, lender participation and borrower type.
Decision it would strengthen: This evidence would show whether credit infrastructure enters actual lending decisions, for which lenders and borrower groups.

When was it measured or observed?2024; cumulative 2021–2024
SMEPS programme reach describes the programme, not all MSMEs in Yemen
The Small and Micro Enterprise Promotion Service (SMEPS) reports that in 2024 it supported 8,217 micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) and disbursed USD 22,865,322. For 2021–2024 it reports support to 31,560 MSMEs and a USD 54.7 million programme total whose status (committed or disbursed) is not recorded in the evidence base. The 2021–2024 total may count the same enterprise in more than one year, so it is not a count of unique firms. These are programme results reported by SMEPS itself: they describe programme reach and finance, not national MSME prevalence or financial-sector lending.
Who or what does it apply to? Micro, small and medium enterprises supported by SMEPS programmes, and the programme portfolio

When was it measured or observed?2024; cumulative/target 2021–2024
The SMEPS financial-services KPI is a programme result, not a national MSME rate
SMEPS's 2024 Annual Report reports that 19% of supported MSMEs accessed financial services in 2024, while the 2021–2024 total reported as achieved is 15% against a 40% programme target. The table does not fully specify the metric-specific assessment base or operational definition of 'accessed financial services'. The KPI can therefore be read only within the programme, subject to that limitation; it is not a national MSME access rate.
Who or what does it apply to? SMEPS-supported MSMEs under the programme KPI

Formal firms in the 2022 survey: accounts were common, bank finance for working capital was not
Among formal firms in the 2022 seven-governorate survey, 58.2% (191 of 328) reported a checking or savings account. Their working capital came mainly from internal sources: on average, 69.12% came from internal funds or retained earnings, 16.66% from money lenders, friends or relatives, 10.15% from advance payments by clients, 1.97% from non-bank financial institutions, 1.31% from supplier credit and 0.56% from banks. The evidence base does not record the number of firms behind the working-capital averages or the intermediary question. Among the 217 informal firms surveyed, 80.18% had no bank account; that sample was drawn from activity and location lists rather than a national register. The formal-firm sample includes micro firms with fewer than five employees, and neither sample represents all Yemeni firms.
Who or what does it apply to? Two separate samples in seven selected governorates: 328 formal enterprises (including micro firms with fewer than five employees) and 217 informal enterprises drawn from activity and location lists. Neither sample represents all Yemeni firms.
